pulls.title: fuzz: add a custom mutator for PSBT
pulls.body:
The `partially_signed_transaction_deserialize` target feeds raw bytes to the PSBT parser. Byte-level mutations rarely produce well-formed key-value maps with valid keydata (pubkeys, xpubs, control blocks, DER signatures, etc), so most inputs are rejected early and the deeper per-field parsing is rarely reached.

This PR adds a custom mutator for PSBT which is ported from bitcoinfuzz (with some changes).  The mutator splits the input into global/input/output maps of key-value records, applies the mutations and serializes the result again. The first commit is a preparation to allow targets to provide a custom mutator by adding an optional `mutator` field to
`FuzzTargetOptions`. 

note: LLM assisted on porting the custom mutator.

pulls.title: rpc: Stamp `getblock` OpenRPC result discriminator
pulls.body:
OpenRPC documents `getblock` as a four-way `oneOf` on `verbosity`, but the dump does not say which integer selects which arm. Therefore, clients that expose a type or method per verbosity (e.g. corepc, btcd) have to hardcode that map. This patch adds optional `RPCResultDiscriminator` metadata, emits it as `x-bitcoin-discriminated-result`, and stamps `getblock`. `getblock` request handling and returned block data are unchanged. Now, `help getblock` notes that verbosity 2 and 3 cannot be told apart by validating a response alone. Also updates `getopenrpcinfo` schema text to document `x-bitcoin-discriminated-result` and `x-bitcoin-default-hint`. The change to the schema's format is:
x-bitcoin-discriminated-result on getblock ```diff diff dump.json dump_new.json 5590c5590,5600 < ] --- > ], > "x-bitcoin-discriminated-result": { > "parameter": "verbosity", > "parameterIndex": 1, > "values": [ > 0, > 1, > 2, > 3 > ] > } ```
getblock description notes verbosity 2 and 3 overlap ```diff diff openrpc.json openrpc_new.json 4696c4696 < "description": "If verbosity is 0, returns a string that is serialized, hex-encoded data for block 'hash'.\nIf verbosity is 1, returns an Object with information about block .\nIf verbosity is 2, returns an Object with information about block and information about each transaction.\nIf verbosity is 3, returns an Object with information about block and information about each transaction, including prevout information for inputs (only for unpruned blocks in the current best chain).", --- > "description": "If verbosity is 0, returns a string that is serialized, hex-encoded data for block 'hash'.\nIf verbosity is 1, returns an Object with information about block .\nIf verbosity is 2, returns an Object with information about block and information about each transaction.\nIf verbosity is 3, returns an Object with information about block and information about each transaction, including prevout information for inputs (only for unpruned blocks in the current best chain).\nThe verbosity = 2 and verbosity = 3 result schemas cannot be distinguished by validating a response alone because a block with no spent inputs returns byte-identical JSON at both levels (a coinbase input has no prevout to add), and the verbosity = 3 schema lists prevout as optional, so both object arms accept both responses.", ```
schema text for x-bitcoin-default-hint and x-bitcoin-discriminated-result ```diff diff openrpc.json openrpc_new.json 8610c8610 < "description": "JSON Schema for the parameter." --- > "description": "JSON Schema for the parameter. May include \"x-bitcoin-default-hint\" when the default cannot be expressed as a JSON value." 8649c8649 < "description": "JSON Schema for the result. Numeric schemas may include \"x-bitcoin-unit\" property: \"amount\" which denotes a Bitcoin amount in BTC." --- > "description": "JSON Schema for the result. Numeric schemas may include \"x-bitcoin-unit\" property: \"amount\" which denotes a Bitcoin amount in BTC. Multi-result schemas may include \"x-bitcoin-discriminated-result\" naming the request parameter or parameters that select among the top-level oneOf branches." 13319c13319 < "description": "JSON Schema for the parameter." --- > "description": "JSON Schema for the parameter. May include \"x-bitcoin-default-hint\" when the default cannot be expressed as a JSON value." 13358c13358 < "description": "JSON Schema for the result. Numeric schemas may include \"x-bitcoin-unit\" property: \"amount\" which denotes a Bitcoin amount in BTC." --- > "description": "JSON Schema for the result. Numeric schemas may include \"x-bitcoin-unit\" property: \"amount\" which denotes a Bitcoin amount in BTC. Multi-result schemas may include \"x-bitcoin-discriminated-result\" naming the request parameter or parameters that select among the top-level oneOf branches." ```
Other results can also use the same discriminator pattern.

pulls.title: validation: bound snapshot cache growth by bytes, not coin count
pulls.body:
Loading a snapshot checks the coins cache against -dbcache only every 120000 coins. A coin can carry a script of up to 10000 bytes. A snapshot file made of such coins can push the cache about 1.2 GB past -dbcache between two checks.

I added a check once the cache has grown by 4 MiB since the last one, and kept the 120000-coin check. Typical coins reach the 4 MiB bound about every 30000 coins. The added cost is negligible. Between checks the cache can still exceed -dbcache by about 4 MiB. I added a case to feature_assumeutxo.py that loads 2000 coins with 10000-byte scripts under -dbcache=4. It fails without the change and passes with it. The coins and validation unit tests pass.

This is one of several PRs from a large audit of Bitcoin Core that I did with the help of LLM tools. The audit produced its evidence all at once, which is why the PRs arrive together. I understand each change fully and will answer review questions myself.

pulls.title: fuzz: Add a target that feeds arbitrary bytes to V2Transport
pulls.body:
No fuzz target feeds V2Transport bytes that an honest peer would not send past the v2 key exchange. I add p2p_transport_v2_receive. It knows the keys of the transport it tests. It builds the input from arbitrary bytes and from the parts of a valid handshake: the peer key, garbage, the garbage terminator and encrypted packets, which may be corrupted. It feeds the input in pieces of arbitrary size. It reaches every v2 receive state and the failures on the way to them.

I ran it for about 13 minutes in total from an empty corpus, with libFuzzer and the address and undefined sanitizers, and it found no crash. Replaying the corpus gets both accepted and rejected messages out of the transport.

pulls.title: torcontrol: send -torpassword hex-encoded to avoid escaping bugs
pulls.body:
The Tor password was sent as a `QuotedString` with only double quotes escaped; as Tor interprets backslash escapes inside it, any password containing a backslash was mangled (or left the string unterminated).

The Tor Control spec deliberately allows the token to be sent as unquoted hex "to avoid escaping issues", as the `SAFECOOKIE` response already is. This patch does the same for the password, and also adds a functional test covering backslashes and quotes.

pulls.title: test: allow slack on rpcwaittimeout wait floor
pulls.body:
Previously, `interface_bitcoin_cli.py` required the `-rpcwaittimeout=5` path to wait at least 5 wall-clock seconds before failing to connect. Under Docker CI load the process can return a few tens of milliseconds early (~40ms observed), so the floor assert flakes.

Fix by allowing 0.1s scheduling slack on that wait floor and reduce `-rpcwaittimeout` to `1`.

pulls.title: net: Use exclusive P2P listen sockets on Windows
pulls.body:
on Windows, `SO_REUSEADDR` does not carry over the same semantics as on
POSIX systems. a second socket can set `SO_REUSEADDR` and bind to a
port that is _already in use_ by another process running under
the _same_ user account. this means another local process could bind to
the P2P listen port and receive incoming connections intended for
`bitcoind`.

this matters because the P2P listener is expected to have exclusive
ownership of its address and port. allowing another process to bind to
it could let that process _intercept_ incoming P2P connections. this is
in a similar spirit to #36169, which made the RPC listener exclusive on
Windows.

to fix this, we use `SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE` for the P2P listen socket on
Windows instead of `SO_REUSEADDR`, while retaining `SO_REUSEADDR` on
other platforms. the added test verifies the expected behaviour by
attempting to bind a second socket to the same port. on Windows, this
fails with `WSAEACCES` (`10013`), which Python exposes as
`PermissionError` (an `OSError` subclass).

references:

- https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/winsock/using-so-reuseaddr-and-so-exclusiveaddruse
- https://stackoverflow.com/questions/14388706/how-do-so-reuseaddr-and-so-reuseport-differ/14388707#14388707

pulls.title: wallet: bound pending MuSig2 sessions
pulls.body:
The wallet keeps the secret nonce of every unfinished MuSig2 session in locked memory for as long as the wallet is loaded. A nonce is removed only when its session makes a partial signature.

I keep at most 2048 sessions per descriptor, about 288 KiB, and drop the oldest first. A dropped nonce is never reused. Its session restarts from a PSBT without our pubnonce. A standard transaction has room for about 1700 key-path inputs. Each MuSig2 leaf with our key adds one session per input, so a PSBT with many such leaves, or several concurrent PSBTs, can reach the limit. I tested this with a unit test that starts 4096 sessions. It fails without the change and passes with it.

pulls.title: netaddress: make .onion suffix check case-insensitive
pulls.body: Makes the suffix/TLD check case-insensitive when parsing `.onion` addresses, as is already done for I2P hostnames. With the current code, a name like `<addr>.ONION` will not be parsed as a Tor address, and will instead fall through to regular hostname resolution.

pulls.title: blockstorage: validate last file and parent links
pulls.body:
A corrupt `blocks/index` can stop the node at startup. A last block file number of -1 makes it read before the start of a vector. A very large one makes it allocate and read that many file infos. A block without a parent, or with a parent at the wrong height, hits the assert in `CBlockIndex::GetAncestor`.

I reject these entries on load, so init reports the usual database error and suggests `-reindex`. A last file without stored info is still accepted when the file before it has info, because running out of disk space while opening a new file leaves that state. The new unit tests fail on master, and the reindex, pruning and assumeutxo functional tests pass. #32427 would replace this database and derive the last file number from its entries.

pulls.title: validation: stop reindex on invalid genesis block
pulls.body:
`-reindex` leaves the node unable to start when the genesis block in `blk00000.dat` has a valid header but an invalid body. With `-checkblockindex`, the default on regtest, it aborts on an assert in `CheckBlockIndex`. Without it, it stays in RPC warmup.

I stop the reindex with a fatal error when the genesis block is found invalid. Its header is already in the block index by then, so the blocks after it could not connect. A new case in `feature_reindex.py` flips a bit in the genesis block and expects the error, and on master it hits the assert instead. The reindex, loadblock, pruning and assumeutxo functional tests and the unit tests pass.

pulls.title: build: Use clang-cl to build on Windows natively
pulls.body:
Building on Windows using Clang instead of the MS compiler may be beneficial, considering the issues with the latter, as outlined in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/31456:

>    * non-optimized codegen: [build: remove need to test for endianness #29852 (comment)](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/29852#issuecomment-2049803970)
> 
>    * compile failure: [MSVC 17.12.0 internal compiler error  #31303](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/31303)
> 
>    * ~legal, but brittle stdlib: [util: Drop boost posix_time in ParseISO8601DateTime #31391 (comment)](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/31391#issuecomment-2510762011)~
> 
>    * unspecified issue: [refactor: Check translatable format strings at compile-time #31061 (comment)](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/31061#issuecomment-2531244463)

Additionally, MSVC does not [support](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/assembler/inline/inline-assembler) inline assembly on the ARM and x64 processors.

So this PR:
1. Closes https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/31456 (and addresses https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/14118).
2. Could be an alternative to https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/24773.
3. Closes https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/36153.
---

Additionally, clang-cl:
1. Produces binaries with [better](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/secp256k1/pull/1681) performance. For example:

| MSVC, block/s | clang-cl, block/s | benchmark |
|--------------:|------------------:|:----------|
|          7.40 |             11.52 | `ConnectBlockAllEcdsa`
|          7.32 |             11.81 | `ConnectBlockAllSchnorr`
|          7.38 |             11.45 | `ConnectBlockMixedEcdsaSchnorr`
|         91.86 |            143.12 | `DeserializeAndCheckBlockTest`
|        121.46 |            189.04 | `DeserializeBlockTest`

2. Builds faster on the CI:
    - [MSVC](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/actions/runs/13792522864/job/38575846787) - 20m 35s
    - [clang-cl](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/actions/runs/13792522864/job/38575849680) - 12m 43s

pulls.title: kernel: Add script evaluation tracer
pulls.body:
This adds a callback hook to the kernel library C header for getting the current script evaluation state on each script evaluation step. This can be used for debugging scripts and gives external applications a view into how Bitcoin Core does script evaluation.

The initial sketch for this work was prepared on rust-bitcoinkernel: https://github.com/sedited/rust-bitcoinkernel/tree/feature_script_debug . That branch also includes a very rudimentary script debugger showcasing the use case for this patch. Clankers seems to do a decent job at coding up prototypes for more featureful debuggers, which seems like a fun project to hack on if anybody else wants to give it a try.

This feature is gated behind the ENABLE_SCRIPT_TRACE flag. To compile with the feature enabled, pass `-DENABLE_SCRIPT_TRACE=ON`. If the feature is not manually enabled, the trace hooks are stubbed out.

The traces are divided into separate frames. RAII is used to guarantee that every script evaluation has at least its start and end state captured. Each instruction generates a unique frame as well.

The ScriptError in the VerifyScript invocation run when calling script_pubkey_verify is added in order to be able to surface the error code in the trace frames.

Another use case could also be using the frames to ensure that the script interpreter is actually doing what we think it is doing during the script tests. This might prevent unit test bugs in the future, i.e. when [error conditions shadow actual behaviour](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/33961), and could also be interesting for fuzzing the script interpreter.

pulls.title: wallet: harden external signer psbt processing, revamp mock
pulls.body:
The current external signer functional test mock can only echo a prepared PSBT. This gets in the way of testing more complicated scenarios, i.e. misbehaving signers and (MuSig2) multisig.

- *test: have external signer mock use a wallet*: gives the mock its own offline node and wallet with private keys, while the test uses the watch-only version.
- *external_signer: require matching PSBT versions*
- *external_signer: merge PSBT response instead of replacing*: tests signers that drop outputs, reduce their value or change the script. Merging rejects these changes while allowing signers to omit unnecessary PSBT fields.
- *external_signer: reject unsafe sighash types*
- *external_signer: **reject finalized PSBT inputs***: keeps the above check simple. Documents this new requirement. HWI does not finalize.

The remaining commits prepare the test helpers and enforce IWYU for `src/external_signer.cpp`.

This PR absorbs the scenarios from #35358, but is better able to test them thanks to the new mock signer implementation.

This PR does not intend to fully harden against a malicious external signer, and can't protect against a malicious HWI (equivalent) process running as the same user.

pulls.title: descriptor, rpc, wallet: do not echo key material in error messages
pulls.body:
Some descriptor error messages quote the string the caller sent, and a descriptor can hold a private key (a WIF, an xprv). The reply then carries the key into places the request may not go: an application's error log, an error reporter, a screenshot shared for help. Even the first characters of a key give away part of it.

This PR stops the quoting.

**Parsing** (`descriptor.cpp`, `util/bip32.cpp`):

| before | after |
| --- | --- |
| `Key ' <key>' is invalid due to whitespace` | `Key is invalid due to whitespace` |
| `key '<key>' is not valid` | `key is not valid` |
| `Pubkey '<hex>' is invalid` | `Pubkey is invalid` |
| `Multi threshold '<text>' is not valid` | same for text of 11 characters or fewer, the length of `4294967295h`; `Multi threshold is not valid` for longer text |
| `Key path value '<text>' specifies multipath in a section where multipath is not allowed` | same rule: `Key path value specifies multipath in a section where multipath is not allowed` for longer text |
| `Key path value '<text>' is not a valid uint32` | same rule: `Key path value is not a valid uint32` for longer text |
| `'<expr>' is not a valid descriptor function` | `'<name>(...' is not a valid descriptor function`, where `<name>` is the text up to `(`; `Not a valid descriptor function` if there is no `(` or the name is longer than 16 characters |

No key is 11 characters or fewer.

**Callers**:

- `Cannot derive script without private keys: '...'` (`rpc/util.cpp`) and `Could not add descriptor '...': ...` (`wallet/imports.cpp`) now quote `desc->ToString()`, the public form with its checksum.
- `Unable to parse descriptor '...': ...` (`wallet/rpc/spend.cpp`) no longer quotes the string: there is no parsed descriptor to print, and the parse error says what is wrong.

Existing assertions on these messages are updated. New tests check that no part of a key is in the parse errors and the caller errors, including a key with a typo in its last character. They also check the exact text of the caller errors.

pulls.title: net: reimplement private broadcast as jobs isolated from the node
pulls.body:
Split out of #36608, the overall private broadcast rework to support ease of review for like-for-like feature.

Differences from #36608 :
1. No tool support or prep refactors for the tool
2. No package relay
3. Slimmed down test profile focusing on protecting aginst IP address linkage and not crashing the node on adversarial inputs (which is a leak in itself)

With `-privatebroadcast`, `sendrawtransaction` queues a job instead of handing the transaction to
the connection manager. Each job runs on its own thread, shares no state with the node, and
reaches the network only through the Tor proxy: it resolves the chain's DNS seeds, then announces
over BIP324 to recipients on a schedule drawn up front, each connection with fresh isolation
credentials. Nothing a recipient does, and nothing the node sees of the transaction coming back,
changes the plan, and the transaction enters the node's mempool only when it returns from the
network. The old private broadcast connections and relay are removed.

The invariants are specified in `doc/design/private-broadcast.md`.

The rest of the tests are in a follow-up to be considered later:
https://github.com/instagibbs/bitcoin/tree/2026-10-pb_reimpl_followup

pulls.title: script: clarify implicit signature-cache input requirements
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Signature-cache hashing relies on input requirements that are implicit at its public entry methods.
Inspired by the Elements rangeproof-cache vulnerability behind the recent [Liquid incident](https://blog.blockstream.com/liquid-network-security-incident-assessment) and the [subsequent cache-key fix](https://github.com/ElementsProject/elements/pull/1600), this change clarifies an easy-to-misread hashing pattern: `Write(data, size)` hashes the data bytes without encoding the size.
Bitcoin Core's cache keys already include the signature hash, public key, and signature in separate ECDSA and Schnorr domains.
Bitcoin Core's signature-cache encoding is unambiguous for inputs accepted by its current script checker: a valid ECDSA public key's prefix determines its length, while a Schnorr public key is always 32 bytes, leaving the signature as the remaining suffix.

**Fix:** Extract the common hashing into one typed helper so changes to the ECDSA and Schnorr layouts stay synchronized.
Return the digest by value from the helper and public `ComputeEntry*` methods so callers explicitly initialize the cache entry, where the previous chained `Finalize(entry.begin())` obscured the output assignment.
Document the existing layout and assert the valid ECDSA public-key encoding and 64-byte Schnorr signature requirements.
The serialized bytes and script validity rules are unchanged.

pulls.title: net: serve `MSG_BLOCK` by stripping witnesses in place
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Serving blocks to legacy nodes currently decodes and reserializes them just to remove witnesses. `MSG_WITNESS_BLOCK` already avoids this work by serving the stored bytes directly. Faster witnessless IBD, as proposed in [#36476](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/36476), also needs peers to serve these blocks efficiently.

**Fix:** Read disk-backed, non-Signet `MSG_BLOCK` replies into an owned byte buffer, check the header's proof of work and expected hash, and strip witness ranges from that buffer in place.

Extract a shared helper so decoding transactions and skipping their bytes follow the same encoding rules. Signet keeps `ReadBlock` for its solution check. Header checks now precede transaction parsing, so records corrupted in both places can log a different error.

**Performance:**

Time to read a block from disk and build its non-witness message:

| Block | Before | After | Speedup |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `block413567` | 1.31 ms | 0.147 ms | **8.9x** |
| Same block with synthetic witnesses | 3.47 ms | 0.374 ms | **9.3x** |

The synthetic fixture adds a 512-byte witness item and an empty item to every input.

**Related work:** This extends the raw witness-block serving added in [#13151](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/13151). The [#13011 discussion](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/13011#issuecomment-383145046) and the closed [#13098](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/13098) identify unnecessary transaction hashing when serving historical blocks. The implementation also builds on the bulk block reads introduced in [#31551](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/31551).

pulls.title: rest: fix getutxos POST body decoding
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Binary GET and POST requests to `/rest/getutxos` for the same outpoints should agree. GET finds the unspent output, but POST incorrectly reports no hit.
The POST decoder writes the body into a `DataStream` with `operator<<`, serializing it as a string and prepending a CompactSize length. It then reads the first byte of that added length as the checkmempool flag, misaligning the later request fields. Hex POST bodies use the same decoding and are affected too.

**Fix:** Deserialize the supplied body bytes directly. Separate commits apply the existing 15-outpoint limit during decoding before allocating the vector, and use `SpanReader` to avoid the extra copy into a `DataStream`.

pulls.title: addrman: apply time penalty in nTime check
pulls.body:
There is an existing check in `AddSingle()` that prevents us from increasing the `RefCount` of an address when the same announcement is received again from a different peer, which regularly happens with gossip relay - an addr can take different routes through the network to us.

However, the check is ineffective: when the entry was first added, its `nTime` was stored with a [2h time penalty](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/9d4325f40316d2c81d34418dc075b235173d0cec/src/net_processing.cpp#L6044) applied, so `addr.nTime > pinfo->nTime` holds even for an identical announcement. As a result, a single announcement relayed to us by several peers could increase an address's multiplicity in the new table, up to 8.

Fix this by applying the penalty in the comparison too, matching the `nTime` update check a few lines above.

This is just a small logic bugfix, it doesn't change things in adversarial scenarios, since peers can just do multiple announcements with changed `nTime` if they want to boost their `RefCount` artificially.

pulls.title: validation: check the most recent AssumeUTXO commitment during IBD
pulls.body:
**Problem:** AssumeUTXO verifies imported UTXOs against a hash we bake into the binary.
Every node reconstructs the same UTXO set during ordinary IBD, but [does not check its hash against the existing AssumeUTXO commitment](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/32377).

**Fix:** During ordinary block validation, verify the provided AssumeUTXO hash when block connection reaches the corresponding block, stopping the node on a mismatch.
Flush pending changes to disk before hashing the UTXO set and comparing the result with the commitment.

Keep only the latest AssumeUTXO commitment per network to limit the extra hashing work during IBD, and update the release process to replace it.
Users who need older snapshots for research or other purposes can use a compatible older release or restore the corresponding commitment as `m_assumeutxo_data` and recompile.

pulls.title: AssumeUTXO: reject duplicate coins and empty snapshot groups
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Snapshot loading doesn't validate the announced coin count against the unique UTXOs loaded.
Repeated outpoints collapse into one coin, so a snapshot can repeat every record, announce the doubled count, and still match the committed UTXO hash.
`loadtxoutset` then reports the inflated count as `coins_loaded`.

Snapshot loading also accepts transaction groups with no coins.
They leave the UTXO hash unchanged and don't advance the coin count, so parsing them bypasses the interrupt check and can delay shutdown.

**Fix:** Compare the announced count with the unique coin count already produced by the existing UTXO statistics scan, and reject zero-count transaction groups while parsing the snapshot.
When both the content hash and coin count are wrong, loading reports the hash error first.

pulls.title: script: prevent partial reinitialization of sighash data
pulls.body:
**Problem:** `PrecomputedTransactionData` could be default-constructed and filled later with `Init()`.
That allowed an object to exist without transaction-specific data and left a public reuse path that was easy to get wrong.
The old `Init()` guard only checked [`m_spent_outputs_ready`](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/2063f02bd5edebe1b5c9635db8850220811ebc90/src/script/interpreter.cpp#L1415), which remained false after initialization without spent outputs even when the BIP143 prevout, sequence, and output hashes were already cached.
No current caller reuses an object across transactions, so validation and signing results are unchanged.
`btck_script_pubkey_verify()` in the experimental kernel C API also copied caller-supplied txdata on each verification call.

**Fix:** Remove default construction and `Init()` so each `PrecomputedTransactionData` object is built for one transaction.
Callers that already have the transaction and optional spent outputs construct it directly.
Validation stores txdata in `std::optional` and emplaces it only after a script-cache miss, keeping precomputation lazy.
`ConnectBlock()` also leaves txdata storage empty when assumevalid skips script checks, covering #35663.
The kernel verification path binds directly to caller-supplied txdata and constructs a local fallback only when needed.

pulls.title: wallet, rpc, gui: Allow users to manually rebroadcast a wallet transaction
pulls.body: From the discussion in #36403, it is clear that there needs to be a way for users to rebroadcast a transaction. Currently, the way to do so requires getting the raw transaction, getting the hex, and using `sendrawtransaction`. This PR adds `rebroadcastwallettx` RPC that takes a txid to attempt to rebroadcast that single transaction. An action is also added to the GUI menu for each transaction to do the same.

pulls.title: wallet: only rebroadcast transactions originating from the wallet
pulls.body:
As explained in #3828, rebroadcast of transactions paying the wallet (but not spending any wallet inputs) is a privacy leak, since anyone can generate these, choose a low fee, and observe who rebroadcasts them. 
While it is somewhat intuitive that submitting transactions has privacy implications - at least until confirmation - this is manageable by various strategies (switching to privacy networks for a while, using private broadcast, making sure it confirms before rebroadcast). However, I find it rather unexpected that just passively running a node with a wallet loaded can lead to a loss of privacy as well.

This PR stops rebroadcasting transactions that don't spend any wallet inputs. For the same reason, they are also no longer re-added to the mempool on startup or after an import: otherwise our node might be the only one still having a transaction the rest of the network has dropped, which can be detected with active probing (e.g. by submitting a child).

This does have the trade-off that receivers (who have an incentive to get paid) will now need to manually resubmit transactions if the transaction doesn't confirm and the sender doesn't rebroadcast, but I think it is worth the privacy benefit.

An alternative approach is https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36380, although these could also be combined (make rebroadcast optional, but never rebroadcast non-originating transactions)

Fixes #3828

pulls.title: compressor: oversized script decoding can leave a spendable script
pulls.body:
**Problem:** The oversized-script fallback appends `OP_RETURN` to the destination instead of replacing it. If the destination already contains an unfinished push, the appended byte becomes pushed data and the result can remain spendable.

**Fix:** Replace the destination with `OP_RETURN` rather than appending it.

Found while reviewing #36280. This predates that PR and appears latent because oversized outputs are excluded from the UTXO set, but it could affect malformed stored records decoded into a reused destination.

pulls.title: http: do not process requests after a closing reply
pulls.body:
The HTTP server runs requests that are already in its receive buffer after it has queued a reply that closes the connection. RFC 9112 section 9.6 says it must not. This is a regression from #35182, which replaced libevent: libevent's `evhttp_send_done()` frees the connection once a closing reply is sent, so buffered requests were never parsed. The server also keeps the connection open after a request with both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding. Section 6.1 says it must close it. Until both are fixed, a request sent right behind a request with both headers is run.

The first commit stops reading requests from a client once a closing reply is queued or the client is flagged for disconnection. Its code and unit tests are azuchi's work from #36355, which was closed. The second commit makes `WriteReply()` send "Connection: close" for a request with both headers, so the server closes the connection. It extends the Content-Length plus Transfer-Encoding case in `interface_http.py`: a `setnetworkactive false` request sent right behind it must not run, and the only reply must say "Connection: close". Tested with `test_bitcoin --run_test=httpserver_tests` and the functional tests `interface_http.py`, `interface_rpc.py` and `interface_rest.py`, which pass.

pulls.title: torcontrol: Limit what a Tor control port reply can do
pulls.body:
A program that answers on the Tor control port can hang the node at shutdown and point its onion connections at another host.

I now accept the cookie file named in the PROTOCOLINFO reply only if it is a regular file. A FIFO made `fopen()` block the torcontrol thread, and shutdown waits for that thread. On POSIX the file is opened with `O_NONBLOCK`, so a swap to a FIFO after the check does not block either.

I also use the SOCKS listener from `GETINFO net/listeners/socks` only if it is on the control port's host. That is a loopback address if the control port is on loopback, and the `-torcontrol` host otherwise. Other listeners, including unix sockets, are ignored and a warning is logged. The program can no longer name another host.

If no listener qualifies, I keep the onion proxy set by `-proxy` instead of replacing it with `127.0.0.1:9050`. A remote Tor whose SOCKS listener is on the `-torcontrol` host keeps working. A remote Tor that listens for SOCKS on another address now needs `-onion`, or a `-proxy` that points to it.

Two cases stay open. A program on a loopback control port can still name a loopback listener of its own, and a regular file on a filesystem whose read never returns can still block shutdown.

Tests:
- a unit test for the listener rule in `torcontrol_tests`;
- a FIFO case in `util_tests`;
- functional tests in `feature_torcontrol.py`, with the mock Tor server, for the cookie file and the listeners.

`doc/tor.md` says that the control port is trusted, and a release note describes the change.

pulls.title: net: add -outboundbind option for outgoing source address
pulls.body:
Closes #6476

Adds `-outboundbind=<addr>` to set the source address of outgoing clearnet
connections, one per address family. It is separate from `-bind`; without it,
outbound follows the OS routing table as before.

- The command line wins over the config file, as for other options.
- Clearnet only: Tor and I2P use their own transport, CJDNS is direct but not
  IPv4/IPv6, and a proxy leaves the option inert for that family (with a
  startup warning).
- The effective address per family is trial-bound at startup, like `-bind` via
  `BindListenPort`; a port, the wildcard, or a non-clearnet value is rejected. A
  failed bind at connect time aborts the connection, with no fallback.

Functional and unit tests cover both families, the startup rejections, and the
bind-before-connect path.

Based on vasild's approach in
https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/6476#issuecomment-1666472338.

An orphan that enters the mempool other than through peer relay (e.g. by

pulls.title: orphanage: Fix orphan reconsideration disconnect hole, add 1p1c invariant harness
pulls.body:
The first commit adds `p2p_1p1c_liveness`, an end-to-end fuzz target for parent and child relay. It
  drives a real PeerManager with real messages and validation, and checks that if an honest peer announces
  the child of an acceptable parent and child, the child reaches the mempool within a bounded time,
  whatever other peers do. Known liveness holes are marked in the target as flags that turn the check off
  once opened, including this one. With that flag turned off, the target finds this bug on master from an
  empty corpus in under an hour on one core; an earlier version found it first
  (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36371#issuecomment-5937814761).

  The second commit hands reconsideration over to a remaining announcer when the marked announcement is
  erased, and removes the flag.

Follow-up PR to fill the holes is here: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36506

pulls.title: net: make orphan reconsideration more granular
pulls.body:
We currently concentrate the validation of all the assigned peer’s reconsiderable orphans that are still missing inputs in a single message-processing turn. This ties orphan processing to validation result, and adds latency to processing other peers' messages.

Always process a single reconsiderable orphan per turn instead. This removes the need for an immediate validation result, and shifts the latency from other peers to the assigned peer.

pulls.title: wallet: Only broadcast resubmitted transactions that were added to the mempool
pulls.body:
As discussed in #36403, one of the issues with current rebroadcast behavior is that the rebroadcast begins an unconditional relay of a transaction to peers. While this is broadcast is limited to peers that have not previously been inv'd the transaction, there is still a privacy leak in this double relay of a transaction, especially so for transactions that are still in nodes' mempools.

This PR changes the rebroadcast to only rebroadcast transactions if the transaction was not already present in our mempool. This provides some additional privacy while retaining intended rebroadcast behavior as transactions that have likely fallen out of nodes' mempools are the ones that actually need to be rebroadcast.

The wallet rebroadcast tests are additionally refactored for isolation so that their behaviors can still be tested after this change. Additionally, a test for the loading resubmission was added, as well as a test for the new behavior.

pulls.title: crypto: plug hardware optimized SHA256 into libsecp256k1's context
pulls.body:
Since https://github.com/bitcoin-core/secp256k1/pull//1777 , libsecp256k1 allows an externally provided SHA256 compression function. This PR plug ours in, so it runs on our SHA-NI/ARMv8/SSE4 hardware optimized implementation instead of the libsecp bare internal one.

The biggest gains are at the signing side, not at the verification side.

The first commits restructure how the libsecp context is encapsulated and initialized. `ECC_Context` now properly handles the libsecp context lifecycle and fully behaves as a singleton, getting decoupled from the `key.h/cpp` primitive (which is no longer accessed by upper layers just to init ECC), allowing us to introduce a verification context within the same object, and moving the singleton initialization to `ecc_init.h` which simplifies usage to a single entry point for all users.

pulls.title: mempool: remove time-based transaction expiry
pulls.body:
This is a simple mempool PR that fixes #33510.

Evicting mempool transactions by age (`-mempoolexpiry`, default two weeks) is
incentive-incompatible: it may drop transactions that could still be mined 
As discussed IRL and in #33510, this PR hence removes age-based eviction entirely.

Transactions now leave the mempool only via size limiting (`-maxmempool`),
replacement, conflicts, or inclusion in a block. The `EXPIRY` removal reason is
dropped. `-mempoolexpiry` is retained as a hidden no-op that warns when set, so
existing configurations keep starting.

Nice side effects:
- With expiry gone, the `entry_time` index has no readers. Removing it saves an
  ordered-tree node per mempool entry and drops a now unused Boost
  include.
- The `DynamicMemoryUsage()` per-entry estimate drops from three indexes to
  two, so within the same `-maxmempool` budget the mempool fits slightly more
  transactions.

pulls.title: Implement BIP 54 (Consensus Cleanup) without mainnet activation
pulls.body:
This implements the Consensus Cleanup validation rules proposed in [BIP 54](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0054.md). These rules are only enabled on regtest. Mainnet activation, if any, is to be considered separately.

This patchset is based on the code that was previously reviewed ([1](https://github.com/bitcoin-inquisition/bitcoin/pull/99), [2](https://github.com/bitcoin-inquisition/bitcoin/pull/110)) and tested (for instance [here](https://delvingbitcoin.org/t/consensus-cleanup-demo-of-slow-blocks-on-signet/2367)) on Bitcoin Inquisition. The tests and documentation have since been improved, but the consensus-critical commits have been carried over with only minor differences (the only behavioural one being the addition of the stripped-size check to `PreChecks`).

Roughly 95% of the added lines are tests or test data. The format, contents, and reproduction procedure for the BIP 54 test vectors are documented [here](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/tree/master/bip-0054/test_vectors). The `bip54_tests` unit test module exercises each mitigation extensively in isolation. The `feature_bip54.py` functional test verifies all of them end-to-end after and prior to activation. For the timestamp rules, it simulates timewarp and Murch–Zawy attacks, demonstrating the new timestamp rules prevent these exploits. A fuzz harness for the sigop accounting logic is also included, which can be seeded from the BIP test vectors (implemented [here](https://github.com/darosior/bitcoin/tree/bip54_seed_fuzz_corpus)).

See commit messages for details.

pulls.body:
The options for wallet funding RPCs have several issues:

pulls.title: fees: validate buckets read from estimates file
pulls.body:
A block_policy_estimates.dat whose bucket list lacks the infinite last bucket makes a later feerate lookup read past the end of the bucket map.

The estimator relies on the last bucket being infinite, so that every feerate finds a bucket. I reject a list whose first bucket is not positive, that does not strictly increase, or that does not end with the infinite bucket. I tested this with a new unit test that changes one bucket of a valid file at a time. It fails without the change and passes with it.

This is one of several PRs from a large audit of Bitcoin Core that I did with the help of LLM tools. The audit produced its evidence all at once, which is why the PRs arrive together. I understand each change fully and will answer review questions myself.

pulls.title: validation: throw when a compressed script can't be decompressed
pulls.body:
`ScriptCompression::Unser` ignores the `DecompressScript` return value and
leaves the script empty on failure, without notifying upper layers about the error.
In the worst-case scenario, which is currently only reachable through corruption,
an unspendable off-curve P2PK turns into an anyone-can-spend empty script.
Given that, properly throwing the error to prevent any future mistakes from
happening seems the sanest path to follow.

Aside from that, added coverage for a P2PK script with an uncompressed pubkey
that has a valid X but a wrong Y, which makes it unspendable. Checking we store
such scripts raw and never encode them as 0x04/0x05, as those encodings
serialize X with only Y's parity (not the full Y), which would make decompression
recompute Y from X and turn the unspendable script into a spendable one, which
would not be good.

pulls.title: headersync: do parameter search at runtime
pulls.body:
This migrates the headers presync parameters (`commitment_period` and `redownload_buffer_size`) from being precomputed chainparams to being computed at runtime whenever a headers sync starts. This has as advantages:
* Less work for maintainers that need to occasionally run the current `contrib/devtools/headerssync-params.py` script.
* Less room for mistakes in that process.
* Automatically adapts based on time (as opposed to needing to predict the lifetime of the software).

To achieve this, the parameter search algorithm is implemented in C++. It is simpler, because it does not attempt to model the fact that the attacker is forced to submit their headers in batches of 2000 if they want to maintain the attack. The old Python code did that, but actually got it (slightly) wrong by missing the fact that attackers are capable of strategically deciding to stop the attack in the middle of a batch (found by darosior).

Unit tests and fuzz tests are added, and at the end the old Python code is deleted.

Also adds a subcommand to bitcoin-util for getting a snapshot's hash_serialized_3, muhash, coin count and total amount values without importing to leveldb first.

pulls.title: build: pass hardening flags to secp256k1
pulls.body:
The secp256k1 subtree is built without our hardening flags. They are on `core_interface`, and `cmake/secp256k1.cmake` passes the subtree only the sanitizer and `APPEND_*` flags, so unless the compiler enables them by default its objects miss FORTIFY, the stack protector, stack clash protection and control flow protection. On aarch64 Ubuntu 26.04 with GCC 15 this also costs the whole binary its control flow property: master's `bitcoind` has no `AArch64 feature` note, and the three secp256k1 objects are the only ones in the build tree without it.

This PR moves the flags back to a `hardening_interface` library, which `core_interface` links; the `CMakeLists.txt` change is a revert of 77e553ab6a plus one comment. `cmake/secp256k1.cmake` then passes them to the subtree the same way as `sanitize_interface`. With it, the same build shows `AArch64 feature: BTI, PAC, GCS` on `bitcoind`. It does not fix #30677 on its own: the depends libraries are still built without `-fcf-protection`, which #30685 tried to change.

pulls.title: contrib: add post-quantum signature tool (ML-DSA-65, liboqs)
pulls.body:
### Motivation

This PR introduces `contrib/pq-shield`, an experimental standalone toolset
implementing the NIST FIPS 204 ML-DSA-65 post-quantum signature scheme
(CRYSTALS-Dilithium Mode 3 equivalent) via [liboqs](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs).

A cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC) running Shor's algorithm
would break ECDSA/secp256k1 signatures that secure Bitcoin transactions.
While CRQCs do not exist today, the Bitcoin Core project should have
experimental infrastructure ready to evaluate post-quantum signature schemes
well before any migration becomes necessary.

This tool is **additive only** — no consensus changes, no wallet integration,
no P2P changes. It lives entirely in `contrib/` for developers and researchers
to experiment with ML-DSA-65 key generation, signing, verification, and key
auditing.

### Technical approach

- **Algorithm**: ML-DSA-65 (NIST FIPS 204, security level 3 ≈ AES-192)
- **Library**: liboqs (C library, MIT/BSD licensed, constant-time implementations)
- **Language**: C++20, integrates with Bitcoin Core's CMake build system
- **Components**:
  - `pq-shield`: CLI for keygen/sign/verify
  - `pq-shield-audit`: validates key sizes and enforces 0600 permissions on private keys
  - `test-pq-shield`: ctest suite (round-trip, tamper resistance, permission checks)

### Testing

- Unit tests cover key generation, signing round-trip, tamper resistance, and file permission auditing
- All tests pass locally on Linux with liboqs built with `Sig:Ml-Dsa*`
- Build verified with CMake 3.16+

### Security considerations

- Private keys written with mode `0600`; audit tool rejects looser modes
- ML-DSA-65 signatures are ~3.3 KB, public keys ~1.9 KB (10-20× ECDSA)
- Constant-time liboqs implementations mitigate side-channel risk
- No consensus changes — this is purely an experimental tool in `contrib/`

### Build instructions

See `contrib/pq-shield/README.md` for full build steps. In summary:

```sh
# Build liboqs with ML-DSA only (minimal)
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs
cmake -S liboqs -B liboqs/build -DOQS_BUILD_ONLY_LIB=ON -DOQS_MINIMAL_BUILD="Sig:Ml-Dsa*"
cmake --build liboqs/build

# Build pq-shield
cmake -S contrib/pq-shield -B build/pq-shield -DLIBOQS_ROOT=$PWD/liboqs/build
cmake --build build/pq-shield

# Run tests
ctest --test-dir build/pq-shield
```

### References

- NIST FIPS 204: https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/204/final
- liboqs: https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs
- Bitcoin Core post-quantum discussions: various mailing list threads

---

**Note**: This PR replaces previously closed attempts (#34607, #36423) which
were auto-closed due to incomplete PR metadata and references to a non-existent
"PIP-2030" (Bitcoin uses BIPs, not PIPs). This submission follows
CONTRIBUTING.md guidelines with complete title, description, and scope.

pulls.title: doc: describe REST browser risk as DNS rebinding
pulls.body:
The Risks section of `doc/REST-interface.md` describes the wrong way for a web page to read the REST interface.

It says a page can read the node with `<script src="http://127.0.0.1:8332/rest/tx/....json">`. A JSON object is not a valid script, so that reads nothing. The server accepts any `Host` header. A page whose domain name is later made to resolve to `127.0.0.1` (DNS rebinding) can therefore read the interface with same-origin requests. I changed the text to say that. A `Host` check would also stop this, but it needs a list of allowed names, so I left it out. I checked that a REST request with `Host: evil.example` gets a 200. I did not run a rebinding page.

This is one of several PRs from a large audit of Bitcoin Core that I did with the help of LLM tools. The audit produced its evidence all at once, which is why the PRs arrive together. I understand each change fully and will answer review questions myself.

pulls.title: wallet: importdescriptors should output the request on error
pulls.body:
## Motivation
When `importdescriptors` is given multiple requests, a missing `timestamp` still fails the whole call with a static error (`Missing required timestamp field for key`). That does not say which request failed.

#34861 is merged. Other parse failures are returned per item, but a missing or invalid timestamp is still a top-level RPC error from `GetImportTimestamp`.

## Solution
Include the failing request in that error message.

## Example
Request
```json
[
  {
    "desc": "wpkh([abcd1234/84h/1h/0h]tpub.../0/*)#x9abc123",
    "timestamp": 1710000000,
    "active": true,
    "range": [0, 100]
  },
  {
    "desc": "pkh(039dcc64c5c644baf0145a5f7322b16399a01a0ee2a182e3150946fe7946358247)#68u5tv65",
    "active": false
  }
]
```

Before
```json
{
  "code": -3,
  "message": "Missing required timestamp field for key"
}
```

After
```json
{
  "code": -3,
  "message": "Missing required timestamp field for import request: {\"desc\":\"pkh(039dcc64c5c644baf0145a5f7322b16399a01a0ee2a182e3150946fe7946358247)#68u5tv65\",\"active\":false}"
}
```

pulls.title: policy: make unstructured Taproot annexes standard
pulls.body:
Make Taproot annexes standard for key and script paths:

- `0x50`: marker-only opt-in.
- `0x50 0x00 <data>`: arbitrary data; other prefixes remain nonstandard.
- All non-P2A inputs must carry an annex, or none may. P2A witnesses must be empty.

No annex-specific size limit; the existing 400,000 WU standard transaction limit applies.

This opt-in rule protects transactions that do not opt in. It does not prevent annex inflation by opted-in participants. Consensus and witness replacement are unchanged.

Builds on #27926 and [Libre Relay](https://github.com/petertodd/bitcoin/commit/04c8e449a34e74e048bf5751d13592a22763ff7e).

Validation: full build, 17 transaction unit tests, full `feature_taproot.py`, and `git diff --check` passed.

AI-assisted implementation and tests.

pulls.title: http: reject Transfer-Encoding other than chunked
pulls.body:
The HTTP server frames a request body by Content-Length when its `Transfer-Encoding` is not exactly `chunked`.

`LoadBody()` reads only the first `Transfer-Encoding` header. With `gzip`, `chunked, gzip`, or `identity` followed by a second `chunked` header, the body is read by Content-Length, or not at all. RFC 9112 section 6.3 requires a 400 when chunked is not the final coding. The server supports no other coding. I now accept only a single `chunked`, across all `Transfer-Encoding` headers, and answer anything else with a 400. Unlike #36243, I still allow `Content-Length` next to `chunked`, as the existing `interface_http.py` test expects. The new rejection cases in `httpserver_tests` and `interface_http.py` fail on master and pass with this change. The framing check in the `http_request` fuzz target needed the same change, or it fails on `Transfer-Encoding: chunked, `.

This is one of several PRs from a large audit of Bitcoin Core that I did with the help of LLM tools. The audit produced its evidence all at once, which is why the PRs arrive together. I understand each change fully and will answer review questions myself.

pulls.title: test: fix TaprootSignatureMsg default codeseparator_pos
pulls.body:
`TaprootSignatureMsg` defaults `codeseparator_pos` to `-1` and serializes it with `.to_bytes(4, "little", signed=False)`, so any `scriptpath=True` call that relies on the default raises `OverflowError`. 81e5c8385b made the encoding unsigned and left this default at `-1`. The only in-tree scriptpath caller passes `codeseparator_pos` explicitly, so CI does not hit it.

Make the default `None`, like `leaf_script`, and assert that scriptpath callers pass it. A call that omits it now fails with a clear message.

pulls.title: ipc: Expose Chain interface to IPC clients
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Processes connected to `bitcoin-node` over IPC (with `-ipcbind`) can use the `Mining` interface, but they can't currently use the `Chain` interface read chain data or follow chain events. Chain data could be useful to third-party clients and Bitcoin Core's own wallet could use this as well to run in a separate process (#10102). But exposing all of `interfaces::Chain` to external clients would make its methods hard to change, since the wallet uses them as internal API (#34981).

**Solution:** Add capnp wrappers for `interfaces::Chain`, split into two interfaces backed by the same C++ class:

- `Chain`, returned by `Init.makeChain`, is stable. It follows Cap'n Proto schema evolution rules, so existing clients keep working as methods are added. It starts with the five block lookup methods: `findBlock`, `findFirstBlockWithTimeAndHeight`, `findAncestorByHeight`, `findAncestorByHash` and `findCommonAncestor`.
- `UnstableChain`, returned by `Init.makeUnstableChain`, extends `Chain` with every other method, for Bitcoin Core's own clients. It can change in any way between releases. Incompatible changes renumber `makeUnstableChain`, so old clients get an error instead of calling the wrong methods.

Methods can move from `UnstableChain` to `Chain` once we're willing to support them for external use. `test/functional/interface_ipc.py` shows a Python client calling both interfaces. Like the existing IPC interfaces, these are only available to processes that can connect to the IPC socket, which already grants full node access through `Init.makeRpc`.

**Merge order:** This depends on bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess#377 and bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess#379 and a subtree update that includes them (this PR currently carries that bump, plus a `-Wc++23-lambda-attributes` build fix that goes with it), and on #36520, which fixes node crashes IPC clients could trigger with invalid `Chain` arguments.

---

This PR is part of the [process separation project](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/28722).

pulls.title: net: option to disallow v1 connection on ipv4 and ipv6 peers
pulls.body:
resolves #29618.

This PR adds a config flag option `-v2onlyclearnet` which disallows outbound v1 connections on ipv4 and ipv6 networks since they're unencrypted. outbound v1 connections are still possible from tor/i2p/cjdns peers since they're encrypted networks.

- v1 outbound connections to peers are not attempted
- v1 reconnections are not attempted (if peer is falsely advertised as v2 peer and we attempt a v2 connection but it fails, we do not attempt a v1 reconnection when `-v2onlyclearnet` is switched on)

Currently 70% of reachable nodes in network supporting v2 (according to https://21.ninja/reachable-nodes/node-service-share/ and https://bitnodes.io/nodes). Also found 81% of addresses supporting v2 in the addrman of nodes I checked - personal node and the nodes in [peer.observer](https://peer.observer/addrman/alice). pulls.title: rpc: add cpu_load to getpeerinfo
pulls.body:
Add a new field `cpu_load` to the output of `getpeerinfo` RPC.

It represents the CPU time spent by the message handling thread for the given peer, weighted for the duration of the connection. That is, for example, if two peers are equally demanding and one is connected longer than the other, then they will have the same `cpu_load` number.

---

Monitoring CPU usage is useful on its own. Also related to https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/31033.

---

This PR uses `clock_gettime()` (POSIX) and `GetThreadTimes()` (Windows). An alternative to those, should this be explored are: `getrusage()` (POSIX) and `QueryThreadCycleTime()` (Windows, but it counts CPU cycles).

pulls.title: depends: harden Linux and Windows packages
pulls.body:
The depends packages are built without `_FORTIFY_SOURCE` and `-fstack-clash-protection` unless the compiler turns them on by default. `CMakeLists.txt` adds both to `core_interface` only. The release flags in `depends/hosts/linux.mk` and `mingw32.mk` are only `-O2`. Debian's GCC turns on neither, so sqlite, libzmq and capnp are built without them. #27118 built libevent with `-D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=3`, but libevent is no longer in depends.

I add `-U_FORTIFY_SOURCE -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=3 -fstack-clash-protection` to `linux_release_CFLAGS`, and the two `_FORTIFY_SOURCE` flags to `mingw32_release_CFLAGS`. Through `toolchain.cmake` the flags also reach the main build. There secp256k1, which does not link `core_interface`, gets them too. #36534 does that for every build. Qt 6.8 already adds both flags to its own targets on Linux. I leave macOS alone, because its SDK already fortifies. Apple clang 21 ignores `-fstack-clash-protection` on arm64. I did not add `-fcf-protection` (see #30685).

In a `debian:trixie` container (GCC 14.2, aarch64) I built depends with `NO_QT=1` and then Core, on master and on this branch. On master no library in depends calls a `_chk` function. On this branch `libsqlite3.a`, `libzmq.a`, `libkj.a`, `libkj-async.a` and `libcapnpc.a` do. secp256k1 is compiled with the new flags. All 380 ctest tests pass, and so do `interface_zmq.py`, `wallet_basic.py` and `wallet_backup.py`. With `HOST=x86_64-w64-mingw32ucrt` (mingw-w64 12), `libsqlite3.a` calls `__memcpy_chk` and `bitcoind.exe` links. I have not run a Guix build or built Qt.

pulls.title: wallet: relax external_signer flag constraints
pulls.body:
The `external_signer` indicates that an external signer device may be called via [HWI](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/HWI) or [equivalent](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/master/doc/external-signer.md#signer-api) application.

When it was initially introduced some additional constraints were placed on wallets with this flag: it had to be a descriptor wallet and watch-only. Also the flag could not be added or removed later.

The constraints aren't a problem for the main supported and documented use case of connecting a single hardware wallet and using it just like a normal single sig Bitcoin Core wallet.

But they get in the way of MuSig2 support, see https://github.com/Sjors/bitcoin/pull/91.

This pull request drops the following constraints:

- `disable_private_keys` is no longer mandatory (but still default)
- `external_signer` flag is now mutable

Changing the `external_signer` flag reloads the wallet so that its descriptor ScriptPubKeyMans are recreated using the new setting.

Additionally it does the following:

- make the `blank` option for `createwallet` consistent with regular wallets by _not_ importing keys from the connected signer
- avoid going through `createTransaction` for external signers (otherwise the GUI breaks)
- create an `ExternalSignerScriptPubKeyMan` when importing a descriptor into an external signer wallet, instead of requiring an additional reload

This should have no noticeable effect on the default single sig use case described above.

Finally we add test coverage for spending from an imported hot key descriptor in an external signer wallet. The wallet signs with its own keys before involving the external signer.

pulls.title: rpc: reset id and version per batch element
pulls.body:
In a JSON-RPC batch, an element that is not an object gets an error reply with the id and version of the element before it.

`ExecuteHTTPRPC` uses one request object for the whole batch. `parse()` throws on a non-object before it resets `id` and `m_json_version`. For `[{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"getblockcount","id":"X"}, 2]` the reply has two objects with `"id":"X"`, one with a result and one with an error. If the first element is a notification, the error is dropped. I reset both fields at the top of `parse()`, so the error is the one the first element of a batch already gets. pulls.title: test: reduce hash mod n for RFC6979 nonce
pulls.body:
`sign_ecdsa(..., rfc6979=True)` in the test framework derives the nonce from the raw message hash. RFC6979 section 2.3.4 (bits2octets) reduces the hash mod n first. libsecp256k1 has done so since 0.2.0. So for a hash >= n the framework's signature differs from libsecp256k1's, though it is still valid.

This is a small, correct fix with a test. The test checks two signatures computed with libsecp256k1, one of them for a hash >= n, and fails without the fix. The change has no practical effect on current tests: the only caller, `feature_taproot.py`, signs double-SHA256 sighashes, which are >= n with probability about 2^-128. If reviewers see no benefit, feel free to close it.

pulls.title: kernel: document process_block storage and two aborting preconditions
pulls.body:
`btck_chainstate_manager_process_block` stores blocks that bitcoind skips when it did not request them. It processes every block as if requested. A block is therefore stored even if it has less work than the tip, is more than 288 blocks ahead of it, is below the minimum chain work, or was pruned before. I document that a caller taking blocks from untrusted sources must apply these checks itself. I leave the header path undocumented, as discussed in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/33822#discussion_r2592425740. #34022, which proposed removing the flag, was closed. Blocks differ because `force_processing` changes what is stored.

The second commit documents two preconditions that abort the process. `btck_precomputed_transaction_data_create` aborts when `spent_outputs` is set and its length differs from the input count. A nested `btck_chainstate_manager_import_blocks` call on the same chainstate manager also aborts. I checked both aborts with a small program against the library. The kernel library builds, and the whitespace and commit-message lints pass.

pulls.title: OP_CHECKCONTRACTVERIFY
pulls.body:
This is a first draft implementation of the `OP_CHECKCONTRACTVERIFY` (`CCV`) opcode.

`CCV` enables to build Script-based state machines that span across multiple transactions, by providing an ergonomic tool to commit to - and introspect - the Script and possibly some _data_ that is committed inside inputs or outputs.

Related to this PR:
- [BIP-433](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0443.mediawiki) ([PR discussion](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/pull/1793)).
- [Post on delving bitcoin](https://delvingbitcoin.org/t/op-checkcontractverify-and-its-amount-semantic/1527) focusing on the amount logic of the opcode.

`CCV` is a general purpose opcode to build state machines based on UTXO; therefore it is not strictly tied to any specific application.

However, as vaults are probably the simplest application of such state machines, the PR also includes a functional test for a very simple (but practical) vault construction, only using `CCV`. More feature-complete vaults are achievable in combinations with other opcodes.

This PR does not contain activation logic, and can't be merged as-is, since it would make the opcode immediately active.

I'd like encourage limiting discussions to the implementation, while specs can be discussed in the BIP draft PR and external places like Delving Bitcoin.

## Challenges with the cross-input amount logic

A challenge in implementing `CCV` is the cross-input amount semantic: the opcode adds restrictions on the output amounts that are inherently transaction-wide.

This difficulty seems to be common to other possible changes in the working of the Script interpreter (including without new soft forks):
- adding batch validation for Schnorr signatures seems to require a similar shared state, like the `BatchSchnorrVerifier` class using a mutex in this [experimental PR](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/29491). Cross-Input Signature Aggregation would also have the same nature.
- [OP_TXHASH](https://github.com/bitcoin-inquisition/bitcoin/pull/51) used a transaction-wide `TxHashCache`, guarded by a mutex.
- [OP_VAULT](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/26857) also has some _deferred checks_ based on information that accumulated during the inputs' Script evaluation.

In this implementation, I added a general purpose `TransactionExecutionData` struct to contain persisting data that is accessible during Script evaluation. This allows the interpreter to cause a failure if either:
- an output's amount is insufficient as per the `CCV` checks across inputs;
- an output is used as a target of two `CCV` checks with incompatible amount semantic.

By the monotonic nature of these checks, it is impossible that a transaction validity is affected by the order of evaluation of the input Scripts. This is an important property for any usage of the struct in the Script interpreter.

As the operations done while the mutex is locked in `CCV` are trivial, it should have a negligible impact on validation. This should, however, be validated with the appropriate benchmarks.

Alternative approaches to the implementation could be:
- a _deferred checks framework_ like in the OP_VAULT implementation. This is functionally equivalent, but I found the approach slightly harder to implement, and requiring more boilerplate code overall.
- making the Script validation sequential for the inputs of the same transaction (that is, distributing transactions to different worker threads instead of individual inputs). This would make any present and future tx-wide semantic easier and avoid mutexes. However, this refactoring might require bigger changes to the interpreter, and should carefully be benchmarked as well.

Finally, there is a possibility that changing the semantic of `CCV` somehow might make it possible to implement semantically (or practically) equivalent checks, without requiring explicit sinchronization during input execution. Here's a [gist from darosior](https://gist.github.com/darosior/ae2108ac0bedd3b68ae047af171b2d44) with some early ideas about using the taproot annex for this purpose. At this time, I'm not convinced that this direction is possible without significant tradeoffs - but I have no proof of this, and look forward to your ideas.

# Related links

- https://merkle.fun - entry point for the resources under the umbrella of MATT (Merkleize All The Things).
- https://github.com/Merkleize/pymatt - Python framework to explore constructions using `OP_CHECKCONTRACTVERIFY` (with or without other opcodes).

pulls.title: util: Abort on failing CHECK_NONFATAL in debug builds
pulls.body:
A failing `CHECK_NONFATAL` will throw an exception. This is fine and even desired in production builds, because the program may catch the exception and give the user a way to easily report the bug upstream.

However, in debug development builds, exceptions for internal bugs are problematic:

* The exception could accidentally be caught and silently ignored
* The exception does not include a full stacktrace, possibly making debugging harder

Fix all issues by turning the exception into an abort in debug builds.

This can be tested by reverting the hunks to `src/rpc/node.cpp` and `test/functional/rpc_misc.py` and then running the functional or fuzz tests.

pulls.title: crypto: optimize SipHash Write() method with chunked processing
pulls.body:
## Summary

The current default `Write()` implementation of Siphash uses a byte-by-byte approach to iterate the span. This results in significant overhead for large inputs due to repeated bounds checking and span manipulations, without any help from the compiler.

This PR aims at optimizing Siphash by replacing byte-by-byte processing in CSipHasher::Write() with an optimized
chunked approach that processes data in 8-byte aligned blocks when possible.

## Details

The new implementation is divided in 3 stages that process:

1. initial unaligned bytes to reach an 8-byte boundary
2. aligned 8-byte chunks directly using memcpy for efficiency
3. remaining bytes at the end

every change was thoroughly tested and benchmarked to avoid overfitting, but replicating is welcomed and encouraged.

## Benchmarks

```shell
taskset -c 1 ./bin/bench_bitcoin -filter="(WalletIsMineMigratedDescriptors|WalletIsMineDescriptors|GCSFilterConstruct|AddrManSelect)" -output-csv=bench_old.csv --min-time=60000
```

pulls.title: log: print every script verification state change
pulls.body:
### Summary

Users can encounter cases where script checks are unexpectedly enabled (e.g. after reindex, or when `assumevalid`/`minimumchainwork` gates fail). Without an explicit line, they must infer state from the absence of a message, which is incomplete and error-prone. 
The existing "Assuming ancestors of block …" line does not reliably indicate whether script checks are actually enabled, which makes debugging/benchmarking confusing.

### What this changes

We make the initial **script-verification** state explicit and log **why** checks are enabled to avoid confusion.
* Always log the first script-verification state on startup, **before** the first `UpdateTip`.
* Flatten the nested `assumevalid` conditionals into a linear gating sequence for readability.
* Extend the functional test to assert the old behavior with the new reason strings.

This is a **logging-only** test change it shouldn't change any other behavior.

### Example output

The state (with reason) is logged at startup and whenever the reason changes, e.g.:

* `Disabling script verification at block #904336 (000000000000000000014106b2082b1a18aaf3091e8b337c6fed110db8c56620).`
* `Enabling script verification at block #912527 (000000000000000000010bb6aa3ecabd7d41738463b6c6621776c2e40dbe738a): block too recent relative to best header.`
* `Enabling script verification at block #912684 (00000000000000000001375cf7b90b2b86e559d05ed92ca764d376702ead3858): block height above assumevalid height.`

------

Follow-up to https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/32975#discussion_r2329269037

pulls.title: More comprehensive datacarrier configuration
pulls.body:
This PR expands the control and testing of datacarrier transactions by decoupling the total bytes limit from the policy configuration.

---

While doing this, the historical **money-first** defaults for OP_RETURN outputs were reverted.

The [motivation](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/33595) for this PR is to continue allowing each node to decide/signal their mempool relay (and mining) policy. However, the open-data relaying capacity of v30.0 is acknowledged and build upon.

The unlimited datacarrier policy is possible with the following configuration:

```conf
# open-data policy
datacarrier=1 # not required
datacarriersize=0
datacarriercount=0
```

---

**But even without the reversion of defaults, the main scope of this PR still applies.**

First, for more robust and complete testing. And second, to allow full backwards compatibility of datacarrier policy. Specifically, to allow limiting the amount of OP_RETURN outputs to just 1.

```conf
# money-first policy
datacarriersize=83
datacarriercount=1 # used to be hardcoded
```

This configuration mimics the exact historical (default) datacarrier policy, which is **not possible in v30.0**.

https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/52ede28a8adb2c2d44d7f800bbfbef8aed86070e/src/policy/policy.cpp#L140-L166

Note that `nDataOut`, which counted the number of OP_RETURN outputs, was removed in [#32406](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/32406/files#diff-ea6d307faa4ec9dfa5abcf6858bc19603079f2b8e110e1d62da4df98f4bdb9c0L162). Without a count check, v30.0 nodes with `-datacarriersize=83` are still relaying transactions with multiple OP_RETURN outputs, transactions which all nodes prior to v30.0 will reject...

pulls.title: mining: add getMemoryLoad() and track template non-mempool memory footprint
pulls.body:
Implements a way to track the memory footprint of all non-mempool transactions that are still being referenced by block templates, see discussion in  #33899. It does not impose a limit.

IPC clients can query this footprint (total, across all clients) using the `getMemoryLoad()` IPC method. Its client-side usage is demonstrated here:
- https://github.com/stratum-mining/sv2-tp/pull/63

Additionally, the functional test in `interface_ipc.py` is expanded to demonstrate how template memory management works: templates are not released until the client drops references to them, or calls the template destroy method, or disconnects. The destroy method is called automatically by clients using [libmultiprocess](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess), as [sv2-tp](https://github.com/stratum-mining/sv2-tp) does. In the Python tests it also happens when references are destroyed or go out of scope.

Commits:

- _refactor: move CTransactionRefComp to util/hasher_
- _mining: track non-mempool memory usage_: add `TxTemplateMap` to `BlockTemplateManager` to track how many templates contain any given transaction. This map is updated by the `BlockTemplate` constructor and destructor.
- _mining: add GetTemplateMemoryUsage()_ - loops over this map and sums up the memory footprint for transactions outside the mempool (includes a fuzzer)
- _ipc: add getMemoryLoad()_ expose this information to IPC clients and add test coverage

pulls.title: [Demo] validation: remove AssumeUTXO
pulls.body:
**Draft demo:** this is meant to showcase what complete AssumeUTXO removal could look like and the simplifications that AssumeUTXO currently prevents.
The decision about complete removal is of course still open. This draft is meant to serve as a concrete reference for the smaller proposals below - it's not meant to be merged.

**Smaller PRs:** I will carve out individual changes to gauge interest in each part, and link them here as they are opened.
Some of the findings are useful even if snapshot loading or background validation stays.
Feedback on which parts seem worth pursuing, and in which order, is welcome.

**Motivation:** this follows our in-person discussion at the October 2026 Core Dev meeting.
My impression was that there was rough agreement about the ambiguity background validation introduces: we trust a snapshot enough to use it immediately, but describe that trust as temporary until the same node finishes checking history.

Multiple chainstates affect much more than snapshot loading: ordinary validation changes have to account for different chainstate roles, candidate sets, notifications, downloads, pruning, cache allocation, database lifetimes and locks.
I am not sure this amount of complexity in the most critical part of our codebase is still worth it, given that adoption [isn't where we hoped it would be](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35054#issuecomment-4468360424).
Ordinary IBD is also getting faster: #35295 is already merged, and the upcoming `pruneassumevalid` will make pruned IBD even faster.

Snapshot bootstrapping without background validation can still offer an advantage: a new node becomes usable before ordinary IBD would finish because snapshot loading time scales with the UTXO set size, while ordinary IBD time scales with the blockchain size.
Whether that is worth its maintenance cost is a fair question, and we can discuss it here or in the dedicated PR where I will propose the removal.
Even after removal, we could decide to add it back in a cleaner way, for example isolated through IPC.
This demo makes that cost, and the code we could remove, visible for that discussion.

**Background validation can be considered separately:** if we keep snapshot loading, I would prefer making its trust assumption explicit and distributing verification across ordinary IBD nodes, as proposed in #32377 and #36543.
That could give us wider independent checking of the commitment without making every snapshot user maintain a second chainstate.

Users who want to validate history themselves and transition to an archival node could rebuild with `-reindex` and pruning disabled.
Alternatively, they could run IBD in a separate datadir while their snapshot node remains usable, then switch once it is ready.
@Sjors's #36557 discusses dropping mandatory background sync and these alternatives.

**What the series demonstrates:**

* After the fixture cleanup in #36601, the next eight commits remove background validation while snapshot loading keeps working, a stopping point that can be reviewed on its own.
* The middle commits remove snapshot imports and startup resumption, then the validation, block storage, notification and release-process special cases they needed.
* The final seven commits add the simplifications this removal enables: startup in one pass, stable database ownership, one download path, a single prune height, and removal of the locks and diagnostics used to select and identify chainstates.

Ordinary validation, `-assumevalid`, pruning, `ChainstateManager` and UTXO export (`dumptxoutset`) remain.

**Related work:**

* [AJ's recent faster-loader branch](https://github.com/ajtowns/bitcoin/tree/202610-loadtxoutset-speedy) and [Sjors's chunked-import experiments](https://github.com/Sjors/bitcoin/tree/2026/10/utxo-coin-chunks) explore reducing import overhead while retaining snapshot support.
* #35054 contains the broader discussion about P2P snapshot distribution, its users and its costs.
